swipes.source: The Wall Street Journal 'Two Young Men' letter — control for ~28 years. Opens: 'On a beautiful late spring afternoon, twenty-five years ago, two young men graduated from the same college. They were very much alike, these two young men…' The difference between them: one subscribed to The Journal.

content.summary: Parallel-lives story lead: two similar people diverge, and the product is positioned as the single variable that explains the gap.
content.evidence: two young men graduated from the same college. They were very much alike…

content.summary: Low-friction trial close framing the decision as trivially reversible next to the life outcome at stake.
content.evidence: Subscribe... and see what it can do for you.

swipes.source: John Caples: 'They Laughed When I Sat Down At the Piano — But When I Started to Play!' Underdog-vindication scene; curiosity headline that forces the reader into the story to resolve the tension.

content.summary: Underdog-vindication headline: social ridicule set up, then reversed at the moment of performance — reader must read on to see the payoff.
content.evidence: They Laughed When I Sat Down At the Piano — But When I Started to Play!

content.summary: In-scene story lead beginning at the social moment of highest tension, not with the product.
content.evidence: Arthur had just played 'The Rosary.' The room rang with applause…

swipes.source: Gene Schwartz-style mechanism naming: rather than 'this supplement helps your joints', name the enemy process ('the invisible calcium spurs') and the counter-mechanism ('the enzyme dissolve'), making the product the delivery vehicle for a named mechanism.

content.summary: Name the problem-mechanism as a concrete villain process, then name the solution-mechanism that neutralizes it; the product becomes the only carrier of the named mechanism.
content.evidence: the invisible calcium spurs… the enzyme dissolve

content.summary: Specific-number + forbidden-knowledge fascination bullets ('The 4-second stretch that…', 'What your dentist never tells you about…').
content.evidence: What never to eat on an airplane…

swipes.source: Dan Kennedy-style price reveal: full value stack itemized with assigned values summing far above price; price then revealed as a fraction of the stack, followed immediately by risk reversal so the ask lands cushioned.

content.summary: Stack-then-price choreography: itemize components with dollar values, sum them, reveal the price as a fraction of the total, and cushion immediately with the guarantee.
content.evidence: Total real-world value: $2,341. Your investment today: $197.

content.summary: Escalating proof ladder: specific customer result → aggregate numbers → authority/credential → demonstration, each answering the skepticism the previous one raises.
content.evidence: Here's what happened when 312 members ran the same play…
